scenes.title: Why February gets an extra day

lines.text: Every few years, February gets an extra day, the twenty ninth.
Why does February get a bonus day at all?
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: Because our calendar has to keep pace with the Sun, and the Sun does not count in whole days.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: A leap day is a small correction that keeps the seasons where we expect them.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: And it really comes every four years?
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: Almost every four years, and that word almost is the whole story.
lines.speaker: teacher

scenes.title: A year is not whole days

lines.text: Earth takes about three hundred sixty five point two four two two days to go once around the Sun.
That is three hundred sixty five days, plus about five hours and forty nine minutes.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: But a calendar year can only hold whole days, so it stops at three hundred sixty five.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: So every year the calendar falls a little short?
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: Yes, almost a quarter of a day short, every single year.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: After four years, those quarters add up to nearly one whole day.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: More than two thousand years ago, Julius Caesar fixed this with a simple rule.
Add one extra day to every fourth year.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: Three short years and one long year average out to three hundred sixty five and a quarter days.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: That sounds perfect.
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: Close, but it is too long by about eleven minutes every year.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: Eleven minutes sounds tiny, but small errors pile up.
lines.speaker: teacher

scenes.title: Eleven minutes a year adds up

lines.text: This graph shows how far the Julian calendar drifted from the Sun.
In the year three twenty five, church leaders tied the spring equinox to March twenty first.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: From then on, the gap grew by eleven minutes every year.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: By fifteen eighty two, the calendar was about ten days out of step.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: So the first day of spring had slid back to March eleventh?
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: Exactly, and Easter, which is set from that date, was drifting too.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: In fifteen eighty two, Pope Gregory the thirteenth introduced a sharper rule.
Years divisible by four are still leap years.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: But century years, like nineteen hundred, are not.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: Unless the century year divides by four hundred, like the year two thousand.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: So three leap days get dropped every four hundred years?
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: Right, and that brings the average year to three hundred sixty five point two four two five days.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: To put the seasons back in place, ten days were simply skipped.
In much of Catholic Europe, Thursday October fourth was followed by Friday October fifteenth.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: People went to bed and woke up ten days later?
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: On paper, yes, though nobody actually lost any sleep.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: Britain and its American colonies waited until seventeen fifty two, and by then they had to skip eleven days.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: Let's put the three numbers side by side.
The real solar year is about three hundred sixty five point two four two two days.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: The Julian rule drifts one whole day every hundred and twenty eight years.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: The Gregorian rule drifts one day in more than three thousand years.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: Leap rules exist to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.
Now it's your turn to test yourself.
Using the three rules, is the year twenty one hundred a leap year?
Twenty one hundred divides by four, so it starts out looking like a leap year.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: But it is a century year, because it divides by one hundred.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: And it does not divide by four hundred.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: So twenty one hundred gets no February twenty ninth!
lines.speaker: student

lines.text: That's right, while the year two thousand did get one, because it divides by four hundred.
lines.speaker: teacher

lines.text: So the next time February has twenty nine days, thank Julius Caesar and Pope Gregory.
